title: 05. LangGraph: Day 9 — LangGraph Fundamentals: Build 2 Productivity Agents
summary: Yesterday you built linear LCEL chains with LangChain. Today we move to LangGraph, a sibling library for when your agent needs to branch, loop, or remember state across steps.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body: Yesterday you built linear LCEL chains with LangChain. Today we move to **LangGraph**, a sibling library for when your agent needs to branch, loop, or remember state across steps. The two projects below — a task router and a standup generator with a human-in-the-loop regeneration loop — are exactly the workflows LangGraph was designed for. By the end you will be comfortable defining state, wiring nodes, and compiling a runnable graph.

sections.title: When LangGraph > LangChain
sections.body: Reach for LangGraph when the answer is not "prompt then parse then done." If you need to (a) decide between multiple paths based on the LLM's output, (b) loop back and retry until a condition is met, (c) hand off to a human for approval, or (d) coordinate multiple agents sharing memory, LangGraph is the right tool. LCEL chains can technically do some of this with runnables and lambdas, but the result is hard to debug. LangGraph's explicit graph model makes these workflows readable.

sections.title: The LangGraph Mental Model
sections.body:
Four core concepts:

- **State** — a `TypedDict` (or Pydantic `BaseModel`) that flows through the graph. Every node receives the current state and returns a *dict of updates*. Nodes never mutate state directly; they return what changed, and LangGraph merges it.
- **Node** — a Python function `(state) -> dict` that does one job: classify, generate, review, call an API. Register with `graph.add_node("name", fn)`.
- **Edge** — a wire from one node to another. `graph.add_edge("A", "B")` means "after A, always go to B." Use `add_conditional_edges("A", router_fn, {"key1": "B", "key2": "C"})` to pick the next node based on state.
- **Compiled graph** — `graph.compile()` returns a runnable with `.invoke()`, `.stream()`, and `.astream()`. Always compile before invoking.

The flow: pick a starting node (`set_entry_point`), wire edges (some conditional), pick an end (`END`), compile. At runtime, pass initial state to `.invoke()` and the graph walks nodes until it hits `END`.

```bash
pip install langgraph langchain-openai langchain-core python-dotenv rich
```

sections.title: Common Pitfalls
sections.body:
- **Mutating state directly.** `state["category"] = "email"` inside a node does nothing — LangGraph only sees what the node *returns*. Always `return {"category": "email"}`.
- **Returning `None` from a node.** If your node returns `None`, LangGraph raises a cryptic `TypeError` at runtime. Every node must return a dict, even an empty one.
- **Forgetting to register a conditional edge's target.** If `add_conditional_edges("A", fn, {"x": "B"})` references node `"B"` but you never called `add_node("B", ...)`, the error appears at `.compile()` time. Read compile errors carefully.
- **Cycles without an exit.** If you build a loop and forget to wire a path to `END`, `graph.compile()` may succeed but `app.invoke()` will loop forever. Always trace your graph mentally.
- **State reducers and lists.** By default, LangGraph replaces fields on merge. To *append* to a list across nodes, declare an `Annotated[list, operator.add]` reducer. Otherwise your history silently overwrites.

sections.title: What's Next
sections.body: LangGraph gave you branching and loops. Tomorrow (Day 10) we close out the fundamentals trio by returning to **Pydantic AI** with two projects that lean into its strengths: a Doc Q&A agent with type-safe answers (text + citations + confidence), and an Action Item Extractor with a `@result_validator` that rejects malformed output and triggers automatic retries. The contrast with today will be sharp — same end goal, very different ergonomics.
